title: Trade winds pile the Pacific half a metre higher off Asia; El Niño lets it slosh back
body: On 12 October 2026, Copernicus reported that September had been the second-warmest September on record, 1.63 °C above pre-industrial levels, with the warmest sea surface for the month ever measured between 60°S and 60°N, 21.05 °C, amid a strengthening El Niño. In a normal year the trade winds blow west along the equator and pile warm water up off Asia, so the sea there stands about half a metre higher and is about 8 °C warmer than off South America, where cold water wells up from below ([NOAA](https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/elnino/what-is-el-nino)). In an El Niño the winds weaken and the warm water spreads back east; the cold layer beneath sinks deeper there, and the rain follows the warmth, which can bring floods to Peru and drought to Indonesia and Australia. In September the Niño 3.4 region, the patch of ocean used to track it, averaged 29.70 °C, its highest ever, and NOAA's [Climate Prediction Center](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml) expects a strong to very strong El Niño through early 2027. El Niño typically raises global temperatures.

slides.question: In a normal year, how much higher does the sea stand at Indonesia than at Ecuador?
slides.explanation: About half a metre: the trade winds pile warm water up in the west (NOAA). When they weaken in an El Niño, much of it spreads back east.

slides.alt: Animation of the equatorial Pacific in cross-section: trade winds blow west and pile warm water up off Asia while cold water wells up off South America. Then the winds weaken, the warm water spreads east, the cold layer deepens and the rain moves east. Then Niño 3.4 at 29.70 °C.

slides.prompt: Weaken the trade winds. How weak must they get before the eastern Pacific is 4 °C warmer than normal, as NOAA found in September 2026?
slides.takeaway: In this toy model, half their normal strength: the warm water spreads east, the slope flattens and the rain follows. Winds stronger than normal do the opposite, as in La Niña. The real ocean is far more complex.

left.label: A normal year
left.text: Trade winds blow west and pile warm water up off Asia. Cold water wells up off South America. Rain falls over the warm west.

right.label: El Niño
right.text: The trade winds weaken and the warm water spreads east. The cold layer sinks deeper in the east, and the rain moves east with the warmth.

slides.label: the Niño 3.4 region in September 2026, its highest monthly average ever
slides.text: Above the peaks of the very strong El Niños of 1982–83, 1997–98 and 2015–16, according to the Copernicus climate service. NOAA found parts of the eastern Pacific more than 4 °C warmer than normal.

slides.question: What happens to the Pacific trade winds as an El Niño begins?
slides.explanation: As the trade winds relax, the warm water they had piled up in the west spreads back east, and less cold water reaches the surface off South America.

source.label: Copernicus Climate Change Service: Second warmest September as global temperatures stay above 1.5°C (12 October 2026)
